notes.short: Six times “whatever”: what to think on
notes.about: Six clauses in a row begin with “whatever,” naming what is true, honorable, right, pure, lovely and admirable. The repeated word stresses the charge they lead up to at the close: think on these things.

original.note: In Paul's Greek each clause begins with hosa, “whatever things,” and no “and” joins them.

notes.evidence: Bullinger gives the verse as an example of Anaphora: the repeated whatsoever things, joined with Asyndeton, stresses the important closing charge to think on these things.
notes.limit: The note is about the repeated opening word, not about any order among the eight qualities.

cites.quote: We have here the repetition of the word “ whatsoever things ” with which the figure of Asyndeton ... is combined, in order to emphasize the important conclusion “ Think on these things :”

notes.short: No “and” between them: a list that presses on
notes.about: The six “whatever” clauses follow one another with no “and” to join them. Together with the repeated word, this puts the weight on the charge at the close: think on these things.

figure.name: Asyndeton
figure.words: whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is admirable
figure.means: six things set down one after another with no joining word, so that the weight falls on the closing charge

notes.evidence: Bullinger, under Anaphora, says the figure of Asyndeton is joined with the repeated whatsoever things in this verse, to stress the important closing charge to think on these things.

cites.quote: We have here the repetition of the word “ whatsoever things ” with which the figure of Asyndeton ... is combined, in order to emphasize the important conclusion “ Think on these things :”

notes.short: Two rows of four: each duty and its praise
notes.about: One reading sets the eight in two rows of four. The first row names duties and the second their praise, and each answers the one in the same place: true and lovely, honorable and admirable, right and excellent, pure and praiseworthy.
notes.evidence: Bengel sees eight nouns in two rows of four, one row bearing on duty and the other on its commendation; set side by side, the first noun of each row answers the first of the other, the second the second, the third the third and the fourth the fourth.
notes.limit: The two rows are one reading of the list, not a settled one.

cites.quote: Eight nouns, in two rows of four members each, of which the one has regard to duty, the other to the commendation of it. If we compare both rows of nouns with one another, the first noun corresponds to the first, the second to the second, the third to the third, the fourth to the fourth.

notes.short: What was “gain” to Paul he now counts as “loss”
notes.about: Paul sets what was gain to him against loss. The gains are the advantages he has just listed in verses 5 and 6, not his sins; for the sake of Christ he now counts them all as loss. They were loss to him because they had kept him from Christ.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: whatever was gain to me I count as loss
figure.means: the advantages Paul had as an Israelite, once gain to him, now counted as loss for the sake of Christ

original.note: In Paul's Greek “gain” is plural, gains, while “loss” is singular: he counts all the gains together as one loss.

notes.evidence: Bullinger (Figures of Speech) lists the verse under Antithesis: it shows that Paul speaks of his gains as a man and an Israelite, not of his sins. Calvin says what was gain while Paul was blind he owns as loss once enlightened, as it kept him from Christ. Barnes: Paul now sees them not as gain but as an obstacle. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) notes the plural gains and one loss.
notes.limit: The writers stress different gains: most his birth and standing as an Israelite, one chiefly his own righteousness.

cites.quote: Note that, by Antithesis, our attention is called to the fact that Paul is here speaking, by the Spirit, of his “gains,” not of his sins. Of his gains, as a man and an Israelite

cites.quote: Those things, accordingly, which had been gain to Paul when he was as yet blind, or rather had imposed upon him under an appearance of gain, he acknowledges to have been loss to him, when he has been enlightened. Why loss? Because they were hinderances in the way of his coming to Christ. … Now he speaks chiefly of his own righteousness
The advantages of birth, of education, and of external conformity to the law. … I look upon them, not as gain or an advantage, but as an obstacle to my salvation.
